chapter_theme: The estate allegory concludes and the body becomes a temple. Thirty-six households of which only two are real householders; one plough and one ox cutting three furrows; an accountant, a bailiff who seizes a third of 21,600 measures of paddy and the gods who squander the rest: the breath spent on living. Then the eight-span house is Siva's temple, with the head as tower, the uvula as flagstaff, the palate as fire-tank, a mandapam of forty-three triangles, seat at the centre and altar at the genitals; such a temple has a gate within its gate, whose lock opens by the silent letter and the mind's eye, and the path runs from the pit two fingers above the manure, past Vishnu's palace and the fire tree, to the six-cornered step. Cast off the gross guise.
structure_note: 2543 to 2552 finish the estate: the households (2543 to 2544), the plough (2545), the accountant and the seizing bailiff (2546 to 2550), the paddy of 21,600 (2551 to 2552); 2553 is a first exhortation to grace-bliss. 2554 to 2559 map the body as a Siva temple; 2560 to 2564 the gate, the lock and the key; 2565 to 2567 the inner path and its stations. All stanzas end with the refrain ஞானப்பெண்ணே.

2543.reading: There are six-sixes of households, and among them thirty-five are foreign households; among the six-tens of households, that one is the attached household, jnana girl.
2543.nuance: ஆறாறு (thirty-six) is the Saiva count of tattvas and ஓராறு பத்து (sixty) their derivatives, together Tirumular's ninety-six. Of the thirty-six, thirty-five are 'alien' to the soul and one (அஃது, 'that') is its own; which one is not said, and tradition would name the soul's tattva or Siva-tattva.

2544.reading: Though all these persons are there, among them only two are householders; if all the others are set aside, those two will raise the crop, jnana girl.
2544.nuance: சமுசாரி is the settled householder with a family, the one who really farms. The two among the many tattvas may be the soul and the Lord, or the two breaths; the song's method is to count and leave the hearer to name.

2545.reading: One plough, a single ox; in it the one beam cuts three furrows at once; having learned, have you seen the cause? Look with the eye of jnana, jnana girl.
2545.nuance: One ox drawing one plough that ploughs three furrows: tradition reads the single breath moving through the three channels (idai, pingalai, suzhumunai). The stanza explicitly makes this a riddle to be solved by the 'eye of jnana'.

2546.reading: The households of the two banks are tax-free grant, and in it the seed sown yields double; the old spotted man of long acquaintance looked it over and went away, jnana girl.
2546.nuance: புள்ளிக்காரன், the man of dots, is the accountant who keeps tally; here read as the reckoner of deeds. The two banks held tax-free, where seed doubles, may be the two channels or the two eyes; the stanza keeps its estate idiom throughout.

2547.reading: Before the spotted man's quarrel could be settled, with the fruit laid down earlier still unhandled, if a palm-leaf order comes saying 'plunder', tell how cruel that is, jnana girl.
2547.nuance: The first line (புள்ளிக் சறைச்சலுமவாராமன்) is corrupt and the reading is a guess at its sense. The ஓலை (written order) to loot the estate before accounts are closed is read as the summons of death arriving while deeds are unresolved.

2548.reading: Even if one stays saying 'it is the fate that came', he demands the bond and the arrears as well; is this his glory, and what pleasure is there in it, jnana girl?
2548.nuance: The collector who takes both bond and arrears is read as karma, which exacts past debt on top of present lot; the stanza's irony (மகிமை, சுகம்) is at the expense of anyone who calls this glory or pleasure.

2549.reading: He orders lake water to be channelled into the box lying at the tree-stump; when they said no tax is paid, he hangs up the worship, jnana girl.
2549.nuance: The stanza is obscure throughout: தரு நிச்சி and பெட்டி (box) are unglossed, and பூசை மாட்டுகிறான் may mean he stops worship or he fastens it. One reading is that the bailiff makes even worship a matter of tax; no confident sense is offered.

2550.reading: He does not let the household stay in the village, stopped them doing service and stopped their work; even when told there is no fortitude left, he keeps on levying the fine, jnana girl.
2550.nuance: The oppressor here has the features of death or disease: he drives the body's tenants out, stops their functions and exacts penalty regardless of pleas. தெண்டகம் is read as தண்டம், penalty.

2551.reading: Of that twenty-one thousand six hundred measures of paddy, did any capital come back once it was seen? Of it he seized one part in three as his share, jnana girl.
2551.nuance: 21,600 is the yogic count of breaths in a day and night, so the paddy is the breath and the one-third seized is the share lost, which tradition explains as the breath that goes out beyond the nose and is wasted. The stanza asks whether any 'capital' (முதல்) is recovered from it.

2552.reading: Of the paddy that remained, the share was destroyed by the madman with the sky-disease, together with Achyuta's son and the sleeping cowherd, jnana girl.
2552.nuance: அச்சுதன் சேயன் (Vishnu's son) is Brahma and தூங்கு கோன் (the sleeping herdsman) Vishnu on his serpent; the madman of the sky-disease is unclear, perhaps Rudra or the wind. The three gods squandering the remaining breath makes creation, preservation and destruction consumers of the body's store.

2553.reading: Did you not see what the land yielded, and will you not look at how it was spent? Without wandering in distress, reach grace-bliss, jnana girl.
2553.nuance: The first turn from allegory to exhortation: having counted the body's produce and its loss, the hearer is told to stop fretting over the accounts and go to அருளானந்தம், the phrase the song uses for its goal in 2519 and 2575.

2554.reading: A house eight spans long, and in it a filth-nest of eight and one; the panchayat men are twice five, and they said this is the city of god, jnana girl.
2554.nuance: The eight-span body is standard. எட்டொரு பீற்றன் மலக்கூடு is obscure: 'the nine-fold nest of filth' (the nine openings) or 'a filth-nest of eight tatters'. The ten who declare it god's city are read as the ten airs or the ten senses, and the stanza turns on their being right despite the filth.

2555.reading: The body is a Siva temple, and in it the head is the tower over the small gate; the crow-like mind ... and the two side-walls are the hands, hear, jnana girl.
2555.nuance: The temple-body of the next five stanzas begins here. காகமன (the crow-mind, restless and thieving) is a stock figure; the rest of line 3 (விரண்டு கரக்கோடுங் கையாம்) is damaged and the reading of the hands as the side-walls is a guess.

2556.reading: The uvula is the flagstaff, and at it is the tower's moon-tank; the palate on the right side is the Agni tirtha seen in the fire-pit, jnana girl.
2556.nuance: The temple's two tanks are placed in the mouth: the moon-tank (சந்திர புட்கரணி) at the uvula is where the nectar of yoga is said to drip, and the fire-tank at the palate the heat that rises there; the pairing of moon and fire follows the yogic map rather than any actual temple's.

2557.reading: The mandapam is of forty-three triangles, and in its centre is the ornament ...; what is seen is in the chakra fort, and so it stands, jnana girl.
2557.nuance: நாற்பத்து முக்கோணம் gives forty-three triangles, the count of the Sri Chakra, so the temple hall is that yantra drawn in the body; it could also be read as 'forty, and the triangle'. Line 2 (நடுவீருக்குதஞ் சிங்காரம்) is garbled.

2558.reading: The seat is at the centre, and the sacrificial altar is at the genitals; in the Siva temple with its storeyed hall the jewelled lamp is burning, jnana girl.
2558.nuance: The பலிபீடம் (altar where offerings are left before entering) at the genitals makes the sexual act the outer sacrifice of the body's worship, and the inner seat (பீடம்) the centre, heart or crown. The lamp that burns in the temple is the inner light.

2559.reading: For a temple made like this, how could there be no gate? Not knowing how it is, they wander about unable to find it, jnana girl.
2559.nuance: The last line (தெறியாமற் றெறிக் தலைகிறாரடி) is damaged; the sense that people wander without knowing the gate is clear from the following stanzas. The gate is the opening of the body-temple, which the next stanzas locate and lock.

2560.reading: A lock is opened by the hand; the mind's lock is opened by truth, or by the body; unable to open the house, they say this is the fate that left them, jnana girl.
2560.nuance: மெய் is both truth and body, and the line works on both: the mind's lock yields to truth, and the yogic reading has it yield to work done in the body. வீடு is both house and release, so 'unable to open the house' is also 'unable to attain release', blamed on fate.

2561.reading: In the gate there is an upper gate, and in that gate there is a small gate; with love look at the tightness of the lock on the holy gate, jnana girl.
2561.nuance: Three nested gates: tradition takes the upper gate as the brow or crown and the small gate within it as the suzhumunai's opening, the 'holy gate' being the one that is locked. The word for examining the lock is நேசமுடன், with love, not with force.

2562.reading: The letter is the letter of silence; if so, it is the good key; if one opens with it so as to free, the way to the crown is seen, jnana girl.
2562.nuance: The key to the locked gate is a mantra that is not spoken: மௌனாக்ஷரம், the silent letter, which tradition identifies with the unuttered Om or the ajapa breath. முத்திதமாக is read as 'so as to release'. உச்சி வழி, the way to the crown, is the goal the key opens.

2563.reading: With the eye, with the mind's eye, if you see that, a way will arise; without taking on desire for women, cherish the way and look, jnana girl.
2563.nuance: The seeing is done by the inner eye, and the one obstacle the stanza names is sexual desire, which 2558 had placed at the body's altar; the two stanzas together make the ascent a redirection of that offering.

2564.reading: Walking with care is the upper gate; how is that road to be known? Without parting from it even for the time of a measure, hear the method of the road, jnana girl.
2564.nuance: மாத்திரை நேரம் is the time of a syllable or a breath-unit, so 'not parting for a measure' is continuous attention to the breath. The stanza promises the method, which the next three give in cipher.

2565.reading: Crossing the pit where the manure lies, and crossing two finger-breadths above its edge, there is the sign where the embryo lies; see that and hear, jnana girl.
2565.nuance: The road begins at the bottom of the body: the manure pit is the anus, two fingers above it the perineum, where the muladhara is placed in the yogic map, and the 'place of the embryo' the generative seat beside it. The stanza describes the body with the estate's farmyard words.

2566.reading: Did you not see Mayan's palace? Did you not perceive the fire-tree standing? Beyond love, past them, is the six-cornered step, jnana girl.
2566.nuance: The stations continue upward: Mayan (Vishnu) presides over the water and the navel region, the vanni tree is the fire centre, and the six-cornered step is the heart lotus with its six-pointed star in the adhara scheme. நேயம் (love) is the attachment to be crossed, or a textual slip for a place-name.

2567.reading: Do not be bewildered standing in the corner; do not whimper while restraining the breath of the whirl; do not dither wandering in vain; cast off the gross guise, jnana girl.
2567.nuance: சுழிக்காற்று, the wind of the whirl, is the breath drawn into the suzhumunai; the stanza warns against both faltering in the practice and parading it. தூல வேடம், the gross guise, is the outward body or the external form of religion; the next chapter opens by taking it as the gross body.

links.note: Tirumular gives the breath in counts by channel: in by the left, out by pingala, held between. Valaisami gives the same single breath moving through three channels as one ox drawing one plough through three furrows, a farm riddle in place of a count.

Tirumular makes the heart the great temple, the flesh the shrine and the mouth the tower gate; Valaisami makes the body a Siva temple with the head as tower and, in the following stanzas, the uvula as flagstaff and the palate as tank. Both read temple architecture onto the body, Valaisami in more anatomical detail.

Sivavakkiyar scolds those who worship temples and tanks: the temple and the tanks are in the mind. Valaisami keeps the temple and the tanks but relocates them into the body, head, uvula and palate; the one abolishes the outer temple, the other translates it.

Sivavakkiyar's mutes pity the whirling gate without thinking to open it and perceive the truth; Valaisami's wanderers cannot find the temple's gate and he gives the key, the silent letter that opens the way to the crown. Both make the opening of an inner gate the whole task.

Tirumular locks the breath in the body as with a bolt and turns the gaze within; Valaisami's lock on the holy gate is opened by the letter of silence. Both treat the practice as a matter of locks and bolts, one closing the breath in, the other opening the gate up.

source_issues: 2547: line 1 (புள்ளிக் சறைச்சலுமவாராமன்) is corrupt; the reading is conjectural.
2555 and 2556: the stanzas end with stray commas after the refrain; 2555 line 3 (காகமன விரண்டு கரக்கோடுங் கையாம்) is damaged.
2543: யஃதொட்டுகுடியடி runs the demonstrative into the noun; read அஃது ஒட்டுகுடி.
